flashcards.back_text: The ventricular wall tension at end-diastole — in practice, the volume of blood in the ventricle just before it contracts. Raised by volume loading, lowered by nitrates and by venodilation.
The resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject. Approximated clinically by systemic vascular resistance; lowered by arteriodilators such as hydralazine.
Chiefly by venodilation, which drops preload and therefore myocardial oxygen demand. Coronary vasodilation contributes but is not the main mechanism.

flashcards.front_text: Mnemonic — causes of a raised JVP
flashcards.back_text: PQRST: Pericardial effusion, Quantity of fluid raised, Right heart failure, Superior vena cava obstruction, Tricuspid regurgitation.
Stroke volume rises with end-diastolic volume, up to the point where further stretch begins to reduce contractile efficiency.
